coverage_window.note: UK-focused run (Sunday morning, covering Saturday 14 November and the night that followed). A weekend window with no CISA KEV additions and no new confirmed UK government incident, so the defining developments are vendor positions moving and deadlines closing rather than fresh attacks. Four entries are new. Rank 1 stays with the Microsoft 365 outage weaponised against UK government, because the thing that was missing yesterday has arrived: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has published the phishing infrastructure - sender domains moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com, a landing domain reallifeaccounting[.]com, the genuine Exchange Online incident reference EX1550543 used as a credibility prop, 'Outage - [six-character code]' subjects, organisation-specific 'Outage Notification' display names, SendGrid click-tracking, and a 13 November variant claiming held messages will be deleted within 24 hours. Those are blockable today. The entry keeps two halves deliberately separate: the email campaign has indicators and is reported as targeting US sectors, while the UK-targeted component - HMRC credential vishing and IT-helpdesk impersonation, with HMRC's warning timestamped 11:55 UTC on 13 November - has no indicators and never will. Microsoft restored services globally on 14 November, which retires the pretext but not the risk: a credential or MFA approval obtained on Friday is still valid on a quiet Sunday. Rank 2 is the sharpest in-window change in the run, and it is a vendor reversing itself: N-able's status page now states it identified Indicators of Compromise on 14 November and is working with affected customers, having reported no signs of compromise through 12 November, with 2026.4 Hotfix 3 pushed to GA the same day - and four published host artefacts (/etc/systemd/system/xvd.service, /etc/cron.d/xvd, a crontab line ending '# xvkeep', user agent python-requests/2.31.0) reportedly present together on all 21 confirmed compromises, which finally makes this huntable. Any UK MSP or public-sector body told last week that there was nothing to report needs to ask again today. Rank 3 is new and is the only UK-relevant incident dated inside the window: Fittleworth Medical Limited, an NHS dispensing appliance contractor delivering stoma, continence and wound-care supplies to patients' homes at over 50,000 orders a month, claimed by Scarlettgroup on 14 November. Confidence is low - leak-site claim only, no statement from the company, NHS England, DHSC or the ICO - but it is ranked third on sector and patient-harm grounds, because the data is special category health data held by a contractor and because appliance deliveries are not something a patient can wait a fortnight for. Rank 4 consolidates compliance and the headline is that two deadlines fall tomorrow: Check Point CVE-2026-123039 with mandatory BOD 26-04 forensic triage, and UnrealIRCd CVE-2026-114713. Barracuda and Ivanti have been overdue since 13 November, and the 9 November batch - now including OpenSSH CVE-2026-123158 'SSHole', confirmed exploited in the wild from 7 November at 00:46 UTC and scoped to musl libc with PAM disabled, meaning Alpine containers rather than mainstream distributions - has been overdue since 12 November. Rank 5 records that the ScreenConnect/SCKit campaign is not over: a second wave on 13 November added 205 hosts across 41 organisations after ConnectWise had already disabled RMM+, taking Huntress's visible total past 490 endpoints and 89 organisations, and ConnectWise is now investigating. Rank 6 is new and strategic: FBI FLASH-20261113-001 states that the open-source agentic AI framework ARTEX has been in criminal use since at least August 2026 against government, finance, defence, energy and health, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours and more than 1,600 operator consoles exposed - which sits awkwardly beside the NCSC's 3 November judgement that AI-enabled ransomware against UK CNI is highly likely within two years. The two are consistent but measure different things, and the practical reading is that resilience timelines built around 2028 need revisiting. Rank 7 is new: Cursor confirmed that a Fireworks AI-exposed access key, plus unredacted credentials inside shared trace data, ended in trojanised Claude Code extension builds (2.1.312, 2.1.313) served from its marketplace cache on 29 October for about 11 hours, installing an SSH key commented 'svc-telemetry' on load with no user interaction - and uninstalling the extension is not remediation. Rank 8 carries Check Point forward with its PHP2Shell initial-access half now much broader: Palo Alto confirms successful exploitation of internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces, and a China-nexus actor chained it with the kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 'Fragnesia' to root 25 Palo Alto firewall and management servers. Rank 9 is new and is honest about what it is not: the Citrix NetScaler November bulletin, up to 28 flaws with nine or ten critical led by CVE-2026-107412 at CVSS 4.0 9.5 against Gateway and AAA virtual servers with no workaround for CVE-2026-19490, is not exploited and not in KEV - it ranks ninth for that reason and is included because this specific product's history in UK government is that the interval between bulletin and exploitation is days. Rank 10 is UK corporate, where the only new GB-tagged listing inside the window is the one promoted to rank 3; A&O Shearman remains unanswered after five days, 118 118 Money has moved into notification with the ICO informed and twelve months of fraud monitoring offered, and Maersk remains the only company-confirmed case. Rotated out with no in-window development: the UK public-sector source-code and Planning Inspectorate credential exposure, the Outlook/Chrome KEV pair (now folded into rank 4), the 'wfx-loot' GitHub campaign (its lesson carried into rank 7, which is the same failure of secrets appearing where nobody scans), and UnrealIRCd as a standalone entry (folded into rank 4). Negative findings recorded deliberately: no KEV additions in the window, no new confirmed UK central government, local authority or NHS incident first reported in the window, and no change in the Gibraltar government cloud compromise where UK NCSC specialists deployed on 2 November.

vulnerabilities.summary: UK government, directly and deliberately - still the clearest UK public-sector targeting in this feed, and now the entry with the first hard indicators. The background is unchanged and remains important to state precisely: the global Microsoft 365 outage of Friday 13 November 2026 (dated 12 November by Microsoft's own incident reference and by part of the coverage) was not an attack. Microsoft attributes it to a technical configuration error during a network capacity upgrade and has explicitly ruled out malicious activity. The threat is what criminals built on top of it, and in the UK that landed on the public sector: NHS England triggered contingency arrangements with trusts reverting to other systems or paper records, the Metropolitan Police lost email and with it online crime reporting, schools and universities were affected, and at 11:55 UTC on the Friday - while the outage was still running - HMRC warned that callers claiming to be from Microsoft were telephoning taxpayers to ask for their HMRC usernames and passwords. The NCSC warned UK businesses about IT-helpdesk impersonation and at least one council, Westmorland and Furness, reported the same calls to residents. What is new inside this window is the thing that was missing yesterday: named, blockable infrastructure. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has published details of an active phishing campaign exploiting the disruption, and the detail is specific enough to act on. The messages impersonate Microsoft 365 service health notifications and cite the genuine Exchange Online incident reference EX1550543 - a real identifier, which is why they read as authentic. Subject lines follow the pattern 'Outage - [six-character code]'. Sender display names use an organisation-specific prefix followed by 'Outage Notification' or 'Service Health', so the lure is tailored per target rather than generic. Three sender domains are named - moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com - with recipient-specific SendGrid click-tracking links leading to reallifeaccounting[.]com. A variant detected on 13 November adds a false scarcity hook: it claims messages were held during the outage and will be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient clicks to restore them. Microsoft characterises the activity as consistent with credential phishing but has not confirmed credential collection or malware delivery, and says the campaign targeted organisations across multiple US sectors - so the email campaign is not itself evidenced as UK-targeted. That distinction is worth keeping clean, because this entry now contains two related but separate things. The email campaign has published infrastructure and US-sector targeting. The telephone campaign - vishing for HMRC credentials and IT-helpdesk impersonation - is the UK-targeted component, and it remains exactly as hard to defend as it was on Friday: there is nothing to block, because a phone call has no indicator, and credentials surrendered on a call yield an authenticated session rather than an exploit to patch. Microsoft restored services globally on 14 November, which closes the plausibility window for the outage pretext over the coming days but does not close the one that matters: a credential or an MFA approval obtained on Friday is still valid today, and a quiet weekend is when it gets used. That is why this stays at rank one on a Sunday. Two things to do, and they are different in kind. Block and hunt the four published domains, the EX1550543 reference in inbound mail from external senders, and the 'Outage - ' subject pattern. Then hunt identity telemetry across 13-14 November for the vishing outcome, which is where the UK exposure actually sits: MFA or device registrations with no matching help-desk ticket, password resets that follow an inbound call, first-seen-country sign-ins, and remote-support tooling started during or after the outage. Detail is from search-result summaries and relayed vendor and official social-media posts; no primary NCSC, HMRC, NHS England or Microsoft page was retrievable from this environment, and the domains below are relayed from secondary reporting of Microsoft's post rather than read from Microsoft directly - validate before enforcing a block in anger.
recommended_actions: BLOCK AND HUNT THE PUBLISHED INFRASTRUCTURE TODAY: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, newbooker[.]com and reallifeaccounting[.]com. Validate each first - they are relayed from secondary reporting of Microsoft's post - then hunt the last 21 days of mail flow and URL click telemetry, and treat anyone who clicked as a credential incident requiring a reset and session revocation, not an awareness reminder.

Add mail-flow hunting rules for the campaign's shape rather than only its domains: inbound external mail whose subject starts 'Outage - ', whose sender display name ends 'Outage Notification' or 'Service Health', or which cites the genuine Exchange Online incident reference EX1550543. Domains rotate; the lure conventions persist.

KEEP THE TWO HALVES SEPARATE WHEN BRIEFING: the email campaign has indicators and is reported as targeting US sectors; the UK-targeted component is the telephone campaign - HMRC credential vishing and IT-helpdesk impersonation - which has no indicators and never will. The staff message is the only control for the second.

Today: push a single short message to all staff stating that nobody from Microsoft, your IT provider or your service desk will call to ask for a password, an MFA code or a sign-in approval about the outage, and give one named internal channel for verifying any such call. Outage-themed voice phishing works on recency, so the message loses value every hour it waits.

Hunt identity telemetry across 13-14 November for the signature of a successful voice-phishing call: a password change, an MFA method registration or a device registration that follows an inbound phone call, and successful sign-ins from a new country, new device or new autonomous system inside the outage window.

Hunt for remote-support tooling installed or launched during and after the outage - Quick Assist, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, LogMeIn, ScreenConnect, Zoho Assist - especially where no change record exists. A caller talking a user through installing a 'Microsoft support' tool is the most common next step after the pretext lands.

Freeze and review help-desk credential-reset and MFA-reset workflows for the outage period: require a callback to a known number or a manager attestation before any reset, and retrospectively audit every reset performed on 13 and 14 November.

For HMRC and other government service credentials specifically, treat any account whose holder reports such a call as compromised: reset the credential, revoke sessions and check for changed bank or contact details rather than relying on the user's belief that they gave nothing away.

Tell finance and payroll teams explicitly that the outage is also a pretext for invoice and payment-diversion fraud, and that no bank-detail change may be actioned on the basis of email or phone contact made during the disruption window.

Report scam calls through GOV.UK and Action Fraud (actionfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040) and suspicious texts to 60599, and record them internally so that volume - not just individual incidents - becomes visible to your security team.

Separate the resilience lesson from the security one and record it while it is fresh: which services degraded, whether paper fallback actually worked, and whether your incident comms depend on the same tenant that failed. NHS trusts, forces and councils reverting to paper is a continuity finding, not a cyber finding, but both land on the same risk register.

Do not treat the outage as evidence of attack, and say so internally - Microsoft attributes it to a configuration error during a network capacity upgrade and has ruled out malicious activity. Speculation linking it to the Outlook zero-day at rank 8 is unsupported and wastes responder attention.

Microsoft restored Microsoft 365 services globally on 14 November, so retire the outage pretext from your awareness messaging this week - but do not close the incident. Credentials, MFA approvals and remote-support sessions obtained on Friday 13 November remain valid, and a quiet weekend is when they get used.
Retrospectively audit every help-desk credential reset and MFA re-registration performed on 13 and 14 November against a ticket, and require callback verification on all future ones.

vulnerabilities.title: N-able N-central '4EverAble2Shell': the Vendor Position Flipped Inside This Window - N-able Identified Indicators of Compromise on 14 November and Is Working With Affected Customers, Hotfix 3 Pushed to GA the Same Day, and Four Published Host Artefacts Now Exist to Hunt For
affected_products: N-able N-central - cloud-hosted instances (N-able has disabled cloud services)
N-able N-central on-premises servers with the Legacy API enabled (non-default)
N-central 2026.4.1.26 Hotfix 2 (HF2) - 19 of 21 reported compromised servers were on this build, so HF2 is not a fix for this chain
N-central Windows Agent and Probe (the separate 'Agent2Shell' chains, to SYSTEM)
Downstream: every endpoint managed by a compromised N-central server
vulnerabilities.summary: UK managed service providers and, through them, UK local government, schools, multi-academy trusts, NHS primary care and the SME supply chain into central government. This is the entry with the sharpest in-window change, and the change is the vendor's own position. On 12 November 2026 researcher Sean Bales published proof-of-concept code for a chain tracked as '4EverAble2Shell'; first exploitation attempts followed roughly five hours later. Stage one is CVE-2026-90436, a critical flaw in the end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x SOAP engine that N-central exposes through its Legacy API, yielding command execution as the 'nable' service account; stage two escalates on the N-central server itself. Huntress reported XMRig cryptomining on 21 compromised production servers, of which 19 were already running 2026.4 Hotfix 2 - which is why 'we applied the hotfix' is not an answer to this. Through 12 November N-able's public position was that it had seen no signs of compromise. Inside this window that changed: N-able's status page now states that it identified Indicators of Compromise on 14 November 2026 and is working with the affected customers, and that it was completing and targeting general availability of 2026.4 Hotfix 3 the same day. For any UK MSP or public-sector body that asked its provider last week and was told there was nothing to report, the correct reading is that the question needs asking again today, because the vendor's answer has changed. The second in-window development is that there is now something concrete to hunt for. Four host artefacts have been published in third-party reporting, and all four were reportedly present simultaneously on all 21 confirmed compromises - which makes them a usable high-confidence detection set rather than individual weak signals: a systemd persistence unit at /etc/systemd/system/xvd.service, a cron file at /etc/cron.d/xvd, a crontab line ending in the comment '# xvkeep', and HTTP requests bearing the user agent python-requests/2.31.0. Huntress additionally advises reviewing N-central servers for the XMRig miner, unrecognised scripts and related artefacts. The exposure condition remains a non-default configuration: the Legacy API enabled and exposed to the public internet. N-able states that hosted N-central environments are not vulnerable - although it had earlier taken cloud N-central offline, so treat the hosted reassurance as current rather than as having applied throughout. Disabling the Legacy API is still the control that removes exposure, and it is available immediately where a hotfix window is not. Two caveats to carry. Neither N-able nor CISA has confirmed the broader exploitation reports: the 21-server figure and the artefact list come from security researchers and vendors other than N-able, none of the related CVEs is in the CISA KEV catalogue, and one source as of 14 November still described no patch as available for the chain while the vendor was shipping HF3 - a contradiction that most likely reflects reporting lag rather than a dispute. The judgement that should not be softened is the one about the payload. Coin mining is the observed objective and it is the least interesting thing about this: the access obtained is root on a management plane that reaches every customer endpoint the provider administers. A miner is what an opportunistic operator does with access a ransomware affiliate would use differently, and the gap between those two outcomes is a decision somebody else has already made or has yet to make. Read this with rank 5: two mainstream MSP remote-management platforms compromised inside five days is a pattern in the attack surface, and it falls squarely inside the managed-provider dependency the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill is intended to regulate. Detail is from search-result summaries; neither the N-able advisory and status page nor the Huntress research was retrievable directly from this environment.
recommended_actions: ASK YOUR PROVIDER AGAIN TODAY, IN WRITING - the vendor's answer changed inside this window. N-able identified Indicators of Compromise on 14 November and is working with affected customers, having previously reported no signs of compromise. A reassurance obtained last week is out of date.

HUNT THE FOUR PUBLISHED ARTEFACTS on every N-central server: /etc/systemd/system/xvd.service, /etc/cron.d/xvd, a crontab line ending '# xvkeep', and HTTP requests with user agent python-requests/2.31.0 against Legacy API paths. All four were reportedly present together on all 21 confirmed compromises, so any hit is grounds to isolate the server and treat it as fully compromised.

Apply N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 (GA targeted 14 November 2026) - and do not treat Hotfix 2 as protection, because 19 of the 21 reported compromised servers were already running it. Disabling the Legacy API remains the control that removes exposure and is available immediately where a hotfix window is not.

Establish today whether any N-central server in your estate, or any run by a provider with access to it, has the Legacy API enabled. If it does, disable it - that is the single control that removes exposure to the 4EverAble2Shell chain according to Huntress's review.

If the Legacy API was ever enabled and reachable, assume compromise and hunt from 11 November 2026 onward rather than waiting for a vendor fix. N-able's own position moved from 'no signs of compromise' on 12 November to publishing indicators on 13 November.

Keep N-central servers off the public internet entirely and restrict management access to a VPN or jump host until a server-side fix ships; N-able has taken its own cloud services offline, which is the strongest available statement about residual risk.

Hunt the published host artefacts on Linux N-central servers: an unexpected xvd.service systemd unit, files under /tmp/.xvd and /var/tmp/.xvd, and cryptominer processes consuming around half the available CPU cores.
Do not treat Hotfix 2 as remediation. 19 of the 21 reported compromised servers were already on 2026.4.1.26 HF2, so patch level is not evidence of safety here - configuration state is.

Hunt managed Windows endpoints for the Agent2Shell chains separately: processes spawned as SYSTEM by the N-central agent or probe service, and agent-delivered script execution that does not reconcile against your provider's change record.
Rotate N-central credentials, API tokens and integration secrets (including the Intune integration) for any server that was exposed, and force re-authentication for technician accounts.

Ask every MSP and IT outsourcer in writing, alongside the ScreenConnect questions at rank 3, whether they run N-central, whether it is cloud-hosted or on-premises, whether the Legacy API was enabled, and what they found when they checked against N-able's indicators. Treat a non-answer as a yes.
Obtain and ingest the N-able and Huntress indicator lists directly from the vendor advisory - they are more current and more complete than any relayed summary, including this one.

Also hunt the earlier-reported artefacts alongside the four above: files under /tmp/.xvd or /var/tmp/.xvd, XMRig miner processes, and unrecognised scripts on the N-central host, from 11 November onward.

Treat a confirmed miner as a pre-ransomware foothold on a management plane with downstream customer exposure, not as a nuisance to clean up: the access obtained is root on a system that reaches every endpoint the provider administers.

kql.name: Published 4EverAble2Shell host persistence artefacts on N-central servers
kql.description: Untested. Hunts the three file-based artefacts reported present on all 21 confirmed compromises. A hit on any one is grounds to isolate the server and treat it as fully compromised; a hit on more than one is near-conclusive.
kql.query:
let Artefacts = dynamic(["xvd.service", "xvd", "xvkeep"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "/etc/systemd/system" and FileName has "xvd")
    or (FolderPath has "/etc/cron.d" and FileName has "xvd")
    or FileName has_any (Artefacts)
    or FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/.xvd", "/var/tmp/.xvd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp asc

kql.name: xvkeep crontab entry and xvd service activity in system logs
kql.description: Untested. Where endpoint telemetry does not cover the N-central host, syslog from cron and systemd is the fallback. Search for the literal persistence names rather than for miner behaviour, which may be throttled or scheduled.
kql.query:
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("xvd.service", "xvkeep", "/etc/cron.d/xvd", "xvd")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated asc

kql.name: python-requests user agent against N-central Legacy API paths

| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestClientApplication has "python-requests"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/dms", "/dms2", "/services/", "/axis", "/ncentral", "SOAP", "/api/")
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(RequestURL, 25), Agents = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP
| order by Requests desc

let NAgent = dynamic(["agent.exe", "n-central agent.exe", "nagent.exe", "nableagent.exe", "winagent.exe", "nablerm.exe", "filecacheserviceagent.exe", "requesthandleragent.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where tolower(InitiatingProcessFileName) in (NAgent) or tolower(InitiatingProcessFolderPath) has_any ("n-able", "n-central", "nablermm", "windows agent\\")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe", "regsvr32.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "msiexec.exe")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AsSystem, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName
| order by AsSystem desc, Timestamp desc

vulnerabilities.title: Fittleworth Medical, an NHS Dispensing Appliance Contractor Delivering 50,000+ Orders a Month, Claimed by the Scarlettgroup Ransomware Operation on 14 November - the Only New UK-Relevant Incident Dated Inside the Window, and It Sits in the NHS Supply Chain
vulnerabilities.vendor: Fittleworth Medical Limited (UK) / Scarlettgroup ransomware operation
affected_products: fittleworth.com - Fittleworth Medical Limited, UK dispensing appliance contractor (DAC) delivering stoma, ostomy, continence, catheter, tracheostomy and wound-care supplies to patients' homes
NHS prescription fulfilment pathway for appliance users - Fittleworth operates as an NHS dispensing appliance contractor, so the data at risk is NHS patient data held by a private contractor
Downstream: NHS trusts, GP practices and community/specialist nurses that refer patients to Fittleworth and exchange prescription and clinical contact data with it
vulnerabilities.summary: UK health, and through it UK government: this is the only new UK-relevant incident with a date inside this window, and the reason it ranks third rather than tenth is the sector it sits in. On 14 November 2026 a leak-site aggregator recorded fittleworth.com as claimed by the Scarlettgroup ransomware operation, with an estimated attack date of the same day. Fittleworth Medical Limited is a UK dispensing appliance contractor - an NHS-contracted provider that receives prescriptions and delivers stoma, ostomy, continence, catheter, tracheostomy and wound-care products directly to patients' homes, by its own account more than 50,000 orders a month. That makes the data held by this company NHS patient data in all but contractual form: names, home addresses, telephone numbers, prescription and appliance details, and the clinical fact of having a stoma, a catheter or a chronic wound. Appliance-type data is among the most directly identifying health data there is, and it concerns a patient population that is disproportionately elderly, disabled or recently post-surgical - precisely the group most exposed to follow-on fraud and to the distress of disclosure. Two consequences follow if the claim is true, and they are different in kind. The first is a data-protection and patient-harm consequence running through the NHS rather than around it: an incident at a DAC is reportable to the ICO and is the kind of event NHS England's supplier assurance work has been focused on, and affected patients will be contacted by the NHS or by their clinicians, not only by the company. The second is a continuity consequence that is easy to underrate. Home delivery of appliances is not an elective convenience - a patient who does not receive stoma bags or catheters cannot wait a fortnight - so any encryption of order-management or delivery systems becomes a clinical problem within days, and the fallback is community pharmacy and trust-held stock that has not been planned for this volume. Now the caveats, which are substantial and must travel with the finding. This is an unverified criminal claim on a leak site and nothing more. No statement from Fittleworth, from NHS England, from the Department of Health and Social Care or from the ICO was located; no press coverage was located; the company's website was still serving normally in the retrieved results; and the aggregator's 'estimated attack date' is a tracker field, not a forensic determination. The group itself is lightly documented: the same aggregator shows Scarlettgroup listing a US hospital (rrh.org) on 9 November 2026, which suggests a current operator with an appetite for healthcare targets, but the operation does not have the established public track record that would make a listing self-corroborating, and this feed has recorded other groups in recent windows whose claims turned out to be fabricated or mis-tagged. Treat this entry as early warning that justifies a supplier-assurance phone call and a contract-register check today, not as a confirmed breach. The right action for an NHS body is not to wait for confirmation: identify whether you refer patients to this DAC, ask the question in writing, and confirm what continuity arrangements exist for appliance supply if the company's order systems are unavailable next week. Detail is from search-result summaries only; the leak-site listing itself was not retrieved, and no primary source was reachable from this environment.
recommended_actions: NHS trusts, ICBs and GP practices: check your contract and referral registers today for Fittleworth Medical Limited or 'Fittleworth' as a dispensing appliance contractor, and identify how many of your patients receive appliances through it.

Ask the supplier two questions in writing, today: has an information security incident occurred, and has it been reported to the ICO and to NHS England. Treat a non-answer or an unusually slow answer as a working assumption that something has happened.

Plan appliance-supply continuity now rather than after a confirmation: stoma, catheter and wound-care deliveries cannot slip by weeks. Identify alternative DACs and community pharmacy routes, and check trust-held stock against the volume that would transfer if home delivery stopped.

Prepare, but do not yet send, patient communications. If the claim is substantiated, the affected cohort is elderly, disabled and post-surgical patients who will be targeted by follow-on fraud - a pre-agreed message about what the NHS will and will not ask them for by phone is the control that limits the second-stage harm.

Warn clinical and administrative staff that any inbound call referencing an appliance delivery problem, a prescription re-confirmation or an account verification should be treated as potentially fraudulent until the position is clear; this is the same vishing pattern as the Microsoft 365 outage abuse at rank 1 and the same staff message covers both.

Hunt your own identity and email telemetry for authentication and mail flow involving the supplier's domain: a compromise at a DAC yields mailbox access that is used to invoice and to phish the NHS bodies on the other side of the relationship.

Do not pay, do not engage, and do not visit the leak-site infrastructure from corporate networks; if you are the supplier or its IT provider, preserve evidence before rebuilding and report to the NCSC and ICO on the statutory timeline.
Record the claim in your supplier risk register with its confidence level stated as low, so that it is not later cited internally as an established breach on the strength of this feed.

kql.name: Inbound and outbound mail involving the named supplier domain
kql.description: Untested. First check for an NHS body with this supplier: a compromised supplier mailbox is used to phish and to redirect invoices. Widen the domain list to every dispensing appliance contractor in your contract register, not just this one.
kql.query:
let SupplierDomains = dynamic(["fittleworth.com"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SenderFromDomain in~ (SupplierDomains) or RecipientEmailAddress has_any (SupplierDomains) or SenderMailFromDomain in~ (SupplierDomains)
| summarize Messages = count(), Subjects = make_set(Subject, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, DeliveryAction, AuthenticationDetails
| order by LastSeen desc

kql.name: Links and attachments arriving from the supplier domain after 10 November
kql.description: Untested. If the supplier's mail estate is compromised, the first visible effect at your perimeter is legitimate-looking mail from a real counterparty carrying new links. Review rather than block outright - this is an operational supply relationship.
kql.query:
let SupplierDomains = dynamic(["fittleworth.com"]);
let Start = datetime(2026-11-10T00:00:00Z);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp >= Start
| where SenderFromDomain in~ (SupplierDomains)
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | where Timestamp >= Start | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, AttachmentCount, DeliveryAction
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Guest, B2B or supplier-account sign-ins into NHS tenants
kql.description: Untested. Dispensing appliance contractors are often granted guest access to referral or ordering portals. A supplier compromise becomes your incident through exactly these accounts.
kql.query:
let SupplierDomains = dynamic(["fittleworth.com"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| extend UPN = tolower(tostring(UserPrincipalName))
| where UPN has_any (SupplierDomains) or UserType == "Guest"
| summarize Attempts = count(), Successes = countif(ResultType == "0"), Countries = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion), 10), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 15), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20) by UPN
| order by Successes desc

kql.name: Egress to supplier-facing ordering or integration endpoints around the claimed attack date
kql.description: Untested. Looks for changes in the volume or pattern of traffic to the supplier's infrastructure either side of 14 November 2026, which is the aggregator's estimated attack date. A sudden stop is as informative as a spike.
kql.query:
let Pivot = datetime(2026-11-14T00:00:00Z);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated between ((Pivot - 14d) .. (Pivot + 7d))
| where DestinationHostName has "fittleworth" or RequestURL has "fittleworth"
| summarize Sessions = count(), Bytes = sum(todouble(SentBytes) + todouble(ReceivedBytes)) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1d), DestinationHostName, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated asc

kql.name: Help-desk-pattern credential resets and MFA changes for clinical administrative staff
kql.description: Untested. Shares the detection logic with rank 1. A supplier incident is routinely followed by calls to the customer's staff referencing the real relationship; the resulting credential change is what you can actually see.
kql.query:
IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in~ ("Account Password changed", "Account Password reset", "User registered security info", "User changed security info", "User deleted security info", "Device Registration")
| summarize Events = count(), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by TargetAccountUpn, AccountUpn
| order by LastSeen desc

vulnerabilities.title: CISA KEV Status Board: Two Deadlines Fall TOMORROW (Check Point CVE-2026-123039 With Mandatory BOD 26-04 Forensic Triage, and UnrealIRCd CVE-2026-114713) - Barracuda and Ivanti Overdue Since 13 November, the 9 November Batch Including OpenSSH 'SSHole' Overdue Since 12 November, Four More Due 24 November
vulnerabilities.vendor: Barracuda / Ivanti / Cisco / Openwave / Google (multiple, consolidated KEV status entry)
affected_products: Barracuda Email Security Gateway (ESG) - pre-auth remote root chain; fixed in 9.4.0.030 or later (sources also cite 9.4.0.029)
Ivanti Connect Secure - CVE-2026-118527; fixed in 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6
Cisco BroadWorks - CVE-2026-20320 unauthenticated XXE in the OCI XML parser; first fixed release RI.2026.07
Openwave Webtop (media transcoder) - KEV 10 November batch
Google Chrome / Chromium - CVE-2026-125350 libxslt use-after-free; Chrome 157.0.8103.50 or later
Microsoft Outlook - CVE-2026-124194 (see rank 8)
9 November batch: GPUStack (CVE-2026-102895), SignalWire FreeSWITCH, OpenSSH, IBM Aspera Faspex
vulnerabilities.summary: The consolidated compliance view, and on a Sunday morning it is the most immediately actionable entry in the run - because the next deadline is tomorrow and nothing new was added to the catalogue over the weekend. No additions to the CISA KEV catalogue were identified inside this window; the last additions were the two made on 13 November, which is consistent with a Saturday. That makes this a status entry rather than a news entry, and the status is uncomfortable. DUE TOMORROW, 16 NOVEMBER: Check Point CVE-2026-123039, which also carries a mandatory forensic triage obligation under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, so patching alone does not discharge it (detail at rank 8), and UnrealIRCd CVE-2026-114713, the labeled-response message-tag injection that lets any user on a linked IRC network execute commands with server authority - upgrade to 6.2.7.1, or on 5.x blacklist the labeled-response module and restart, with UK exposure concentrated in universities, ISPs, hosting providers and community networks rather than in government estates. OVERDUE SINCE 13 NOVEMBER: the Barracuda Email Security Gateway pre-authentication remote root chain (CVE-2026-116606 chained with CVE-2026-111560, fix 9.4.0.030 or later, with some sources citing 9.4.0.029) and Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-118527 (25.1.1.3 or 22.8R2.6). The Ivanti caveat still stands and still catches people: an October patch cycle covered only CVE-2026-104935, and the Integrity Checker Tool can return clean on a compromised appliance because attacker commands execute in memory - so anything reachable from an appliance exposed since 3 October needs LAPS rotation and BitLocker re-escrow, not just a version check. OVERDUE SINCE 12 NOVEMBER: the 9 November batch - GPUStack (CVE-2026-102895), SignalWire FreeSWITCH, IBM Aspera Faspex, and OpenSSH CVE-2026-123158, the authentication bypass nicknamed 'SSHole'. The OpenSSH item deserves a line of its own because the exploitation evidence is unusually well documented and the scoping is unusually narrow: it affects portable OpenSSH on Linux built against musl libc with PAM disabled, which in practice means Alpine-based hosts and containers, while Debian, Ubuntu, SUSE, Red Hat and CentOS are reported unaffected and stock OpenWrt uses Dropbear instead. GreyNoise recorded the first successful in-the-wild exploitation on 7 November at 00:46 UTC, roughly 40 hours after the fix, and a separate researcher observed the first attempt under nine hours after CVE publication and confirmed root access on an Alpine honeypot. Current reporting describes the activity as botnets and cryptominers rather than targeted intrusion, which lowers the immediate severity without changing the remediation: OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution's patched package, followed by an sshd restart. For UK estates the realistic exposure is Alpine container images in Kubernetes and CI pipelines, which is also the population least likely to appear in an appliance-focused patching report. DUE 24 NOVEMBER: Cisco BroadWorks CVE-2026-20320 (RI.2026.07 - and rotate the system identity key, certificates and stored credentials, because key material read through an XXE remains valid after patching; BroadWorks underpins hosted-voice platforms resold into UK local government, housing associations and the NHS), Openwave Webtop, Chrome/Chromium CVE-2026-125350 (a libxslt use-after-free, exploited in the wild, requiring a browser relaunch to 157.0.8103.50 or later rather than merely a downloaded update), and Microsoft Outlook CVE-2026-124194 (verify Office build numbers rather than OS patch level, and block outbound SMB/445 and WebDAV; NHS England's own cyber alert CC-4889 of 11 November flags it as exploited as a zero-day and assesses further exploitation as highly likely). Overdue status matters beyond US federal compliance. Much of the UK public sector has effectively adopted KEV as a benchmark through NCSC guidance and contractual terms, and four of the items above are internet-facing appliances with confirmed exploitation - the exact asset class that produces the incidents this feed reports a fortnight later. Detail is from search-result summaries; the CISA KEV catalogue and the CISA alert pages were not retrievable from this environment, so deadline dates should be verified against the catalogue before being quoted in a compliance return.
recommended_actions: TOMORROW IS THE DEADLINE for two items: Check Point CVE-2026-123039 (apply the November Jumbo Hotfix - R82.20 Take 14, R82.10 Take 52, R82 Take 132, R81.20 Take 174 or later - AND complete forensic triage, which BOD 26-04 makes mandatory and which patching does not satisfy) and UnrealIRCd CVE-2026-114713 (upgrade to 6.2.7.1; on 5.x blacklist the labeled-response module and restart).

PATCH THE OVERDUE OPENSSH ITEM, AND LOOK IN THE RIGHT PLACE: CVE-2026-123158 'SSHole' has been overdue since 12 November and affects portable OpenSSH on Linux with musl libc and PAM disabled - in practice Alpine hosts and containers. Fix is OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution's patched package, then restart sshd. Debian, Ubuntu, SUSE, Red Hat and CentOS are reported unaffected, so the exposure is most likely in container images in your Kubernetes clusters and CI pipelines rather than on your servers.

Recognise the compliance position before triaging: the Barracuda ESG chain (CVE-2026-116606 + CVE-2026-111560) and Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-118527 passed their KEV deadline on 13 November and are overdue, and the 9 November batch (GPUStack CVE-2026-102895, SignalWire FreeSWITCH, OpenSSH, IBM Aspera Faspex) has been overdue since 12 November. Overdue internet-facing appliances with confirmed exploitation are the highest-probability route to a UK public-sector incident in this run.
Today: patch Barracuda ESG to 9.4.0.030 or later and Ivanti Connect Secure to 25.1.1.3 or 22.8R2.6. If either cannot be patched today, take it off the internet until it can be.
Do not rely on Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool as clearance. Attacker commands run in memory and may leave no on-disk trace; a clean ICT result does not exclude compromise.

For any Ivanti appliance internet-exposed since 3 October 2026, rotate LAPS passwords and re-escrow BitLocker recovery keys for everything the appliance could reach, plus all appliance-resident credentials, certificates and API keys.
If you patched Ivanti on 13 October, re-check: that update addressed CVE-2026-104935 only and leaves CVE-2026-118527 and CVE-2026-111357 unremediated.

For Barracuda ESG, after patching, review mail-flow rules, connectors and forwarding configuration for unauthorised changes, and rotate the appliance's directory bind account and any stored SMTP credentials.
Hunt both appliances for added SSH keys, new local accounts, modified cron entries and unexpected outbound connections, and compare running configuration to a known-good baseline.

Close out the 9 November KEV batch if still open - it is now past deadline. Prioritise OpenSSH CVE-2026-123158 by scanning container registries and appliance firmware for Alpine/musl builds, not just running servers.
Where either appliance terminates authentication for internal services, review sign-in logs for the period of exposure for successful authentications that do not correspond to known user activity.

Cisco BroadWorks CVE-2026-20320 (KEV, due 24 November): upgrade to RI.2026.07 - there is no workaround - and then rotate the system identity key, certificates and all stored credentials. An unauthenticated XXE read of configuration data leaves key material that stays valid after patching, so the upgrade alone leaves the attacker holding working secrets.

If you consume hosted voice or unified communications from a UK reseller, ask whether its platform runs BroadWorks and whether it has patched to RI.2026.07 and rotated platform key material. Reported exploitation ('Operation Snowball', per Malbear Labs) was against a European telecommunications provider and 13 companies hosted on its infrastructure - that is the provider-to-tenant shape, and it is a researcher claim rather than a vendor- or CISA-confirmed one.

Scan your container registries and CI base images for Alpine images running sshd, not just your host estate. Exploitation of SSHole was confirmed in the wild on 7 November and current activity is botnets and cryptominers, which is the profile that finds forgotten build infrastructure first.

Cross-check your patching position against NHS England Digital's own alerts if you are an NHS body: CC-4889 (Microsoft November updates, Outlook CVE-2026-124194 exploited as a zero-day) and CC-4888 (Fortinet, 98 vulnerabilities including 19 critical), both dated 11 November 2026.

kql.name: OpenSSH SSHole (CVE-2026-123158) exposure across Linux hosts and containers
kql.description: Untested. Scopes the overdue OpenSSH item. Endpoint vulnerability data rarely covers container images, so treat an empty result as a visibility gap rather than as an all-clear and cross-check your registry scanning for Alpine base images running sshd.
kql.query:
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-123158")
    or (SoftwareName has "openssh" and SoftwareVendor has_any ("openbsd", "openssh"))
| summarize CVEs = make_set(CveId, 20), Versions = make_set(SoftwareVersion, 20), Devices = make_set(DeviceName, 50) by SoftwareName, OSPlatform
| order by SoftwareName asc

kql.name: Successful SSH authentication without a corresponding PAM session (SSHole bypass pattern)
kql.description: Untested and dependent on your sshd log verbosity. The bypass applies where PAM is disabled, so the signal is an accepted authentication that is not accompanied by the usual session-open accounting. Baseline on a known-good Alpine host before relying on it.
kql.query:
let Start = datetime(2026-11-05T00:00:00Z);
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated >= Start
| where ProcessName == "sshd" or SyslogMessage has "sshd"
| extend Accepted = SyslogMessage has_any ("Accepted publickey", "Accepted password", "Accepted none", "Accepted keyboard-interactive")
| extend SessionOpened = SyslogMessage has_any ("session opened", "pam_unix")
| summarize Accepts = countif(Accepted), Sessions = countif(SessionOpened), Samples = make_set(substring(SyslogMessage, 0, 200), 10) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Accepts > 0 and Sessions == 0
| order by TimeGenerated asc

kql.name: Ivanti Connect Secure - anomalous authentication and session activity during the exposure window
kql.description: Untested. Because in-memory exploitation leaves little appliance-side trace, authentication anomalies are often the only evidence. Covers 3 October onward, the exposure window carried in this feed.
kql.query:
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > datetime(2026-10-03)
| where DeviceVendor has_any ("Ivanti", "Pulse", "Juniper")
| where Activity has_any ("login", "Login succeeded", "session", "authentication", "VPN")
| summarize Events = count(), Users = make_set(DestinationUserName, 50), IPs = make_set(SourceIP, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, Activity
| order by Events desc

kql.name: Post-appliance-compromise credential reuse against the identity plane
kql.description: Untested. An edge compromise converts into identity-plane access. Compares sign-in ASNs since 3 October against a 90-day baseline to surface credential reuse from new infrastructure.
kql.query:
let Baseline = SigninLogs
  | where TimeGenerated between (ago(180d) .. datetime(2026-10-03))
  | summarize KnownASNs = make_set(AutonomousSystemNumber, 300) by UserPrincipalName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > datetime(2026-10-03)
| where ResultType == 0
| join kind=leftouter Baseline on UserPrincipalName
| where isempty(KnownASNs) or AutonomousSystemNumber !in (KnownASNs)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, Location, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Barracuda ESG - exploitation attempts and post-exploitation command patterns
kql.description: Untested. Looks for the auth-bypass-then-command-injection shape in appliance logs. Attacker IPs from the 9-11 November telemetry were not published, so this is pattern-based.
kql.query:
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Barracuda"
| where RequestURL has_any ("cgi-mod", "admin", "index.cgi", "smtp")
   or Message has_any ("command", "exec", "system", ";", "|", "`", "$(")
| summarize Events = count(), URLs = make_set(RequestURL, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DeviceName
| where Events > 1
| order by Events desc

Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > datetime(2026-10-03)
| where Computer has_any ("ivanti", "pulse", "barracuda", "esg", "ics", "vpn")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("authorized_keys", "useradd", "adduser", "crontab", "new user", "password changed", "chmod", "wget ", "curl ", "/tmp/", "nohup")

vulnerabilities.title: ConnectWise ScreenConnect MSP Console Hijacking and the 'SCKit' Worm: a Second Wave on 13 November Added 205 More Hosts Across 41 Organisations, Taking Huntress's Visible Total Past 490 Endpoints and 89 Organisations - ConnectWise Is Now Investigating the Reported Breaches
affected_products: ConnectWise ScreenConnect - cloud-hosted instances (primary observed target)
ScreenConnect 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783 (both observed affected - running the latest release was not protective)
On-premises ScreenConnect deployments running any of the five 'RMM+' family extensions
Downstream: every endpoint managed by a compromised MSP's ScreenConnect instance
vulnerabilities.summary: UK corporate and UK public sector via managed service providers. The in-window development is that this campaign is not over: Huntress reports a second wave on 13 November 2026 affecting an additional 205 hosts across 41 organisations, on top of the first wave's 288 endpoints across 48 organisations - taking the running total inside Huntress's own visibility past 490 endpoints and 89 organisations, and that is one vendor's customer base, not a global figure. A second wave two days after the first, after the vendor had disabled the suspected extension, is the detail that should change behaviour: it means the access route has not been fully closed, or the attacker retained footholds established in wave one, and either way 'we checked on Wednesday' is no longer a position. The mechanism is unchanged and is not a product vulnerability. Attackers abused ScreenConnect's legitimate Run Command feature to push commands as SYSTEM to many endpoints at once, installing an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client and a toolkit called SCKit, with all of wave one landing inside roughly 90 minutes. Huntress says the activity 'seems to be related' to RMM+, a third-party ScreenConnect extension, and ConnectWise has disabled RMM+ along with four other third-party extensions while stating that it found no breach of its own infrastructure and no flaw in ScreenConnect itself. Researchers at Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber have not observed successful exploitation of CVE-2026-84869, and Blackpoint confirmed the exploit failed against a patched client - so the initial-access question remains genuinely open rather than settled, and that open question is now reinforced by the second wave. Microsoft published its own analysis on 13 November under the title 'SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy remote access and target technician sessions', confirming the activity ConnectWise reported and adding the behavioural detail that matters most for responders: the toolkit is built to move from a managed customer endpoint onto the technician's own machine. Neither Huntress nor Blackpoint has seen that worm-like step succeed in the wild, but the design intent is established, and it drives the single most important operational instruction in this entry - do NOT triage a suspected infection by connecting to the host through ScreenConnect, because the responder's own workstation is in scope. Isolate the host by other means, then revoke sessions and credentials. ConnectWise is reported to be investigating the breaches at nearly 50 organisations following third-party reporting, which is a change in posture from its earlier position that nothing in its own estate was affected. UK relevance remains direct and structural: ScreenConnect is a mainstay of the UK MSP and IT-support market serving local authorities, NHS primary care and dental practices, schools and multi-academy trusts, and the SME supply chain into central government. Read this entry together with rank 2 - two different MSP remote-management platforms compromised inside five days, one of them with a vendor that reversed its 'no signs of compromise' position inside this window - and the reasonable planning assumption for a UK public-sector body is that its provider's remote-management plane is currently the most likely route into its estate. Detail is from search-result summaries; the Huntress, Microsoft and ConnectWise pages were not retrievable from this environment, and the wave-two figures come from Huntress's own blog as relayed in secondary reporting.
recommended_actions: RE-CHECK EVEN IF YOU CHECKED MIDWEEK: a second wave on 13 November added 205 hosts across 41 organisations after ConnectWise had already disabled RMM+ and four other extensions. That means the route is not demonstrably closed, and an assessment completed on Wednesday no longer covers you.

Today: ask every MSP and IT outsourcer with remote access to your estate, in writing, whether they run ConnectWise ScreenConnect, whether their instance is cloud-hosted, and whether any 'RMM+' family extension was installed. Treat a non-answer as a yes and isolate accordingly.

In on-premises ScreenConnect deployments, disable the RMM+ family extensions immediately - ConnectWise has already disabled them in ~400 cloud environments but on-premises operators must act themselves.

Do NOT triage a suspected infected endpoint over ScreenConnect. Use out-of-band access (EDR live response, direct console, separate RMM) - connecting through the compromised tool exposes the responder's workstation.

Hunt for the full set of ScreenConnect clients installed across your estate and reconcile against the authorised instance identifier; a second, unauthorised client is the campaign's persistence mechanism.

Hunt for Microsoft Defender exclusion additions created in the last 7 days, especially any created by a process parented to a ScreenConnect service - this preceded payload staging in the observed intrusions.
Hunt for any process executed as SYSTEM with a ScreenConnect service as the parent, concentrating on the 11 November 17:00-20:00 UTC window and the following 72 hours.
Rotate credentials, API keys and session tokens that any ScreenConnect-managed endpoint could reach, and force re-authentication for privileged accounts used by support technicians.
Obtain and ingest the Huntress and ConnectWise indicator lists directly - they were published with the research and are more current than any relayed summary.
Review and restrict ScreenConnect's 'Run command' capability by role; it is the execution primitive that turned console access into SYSTEM on 288 machines.

Reconcile every installed ScreenConnect client against your authorised instance identifier again, including on endpoints you cleared last week, and hunt for Defender exclusions added in the last three weeks.

If your provider uses ScreenConnect, ask specifically whether it was in either wave, whether RMM+ or any other third-party extension was installed, and whether any technician workstation has been examined - Microsoft's analysis describes the toolkit as built to reach technician sessions.

kql.name: Burst of SYSTEM-context command execution under the ScreenConnect client (both waves)
kql.description: Untested. kql.query:
let WaveStart = datetime(2026-11-11T00:00:00Z);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp >= WaveStart
| where tolower(InitiatingProcessFileName) has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwisecontrol", "connectwise")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe", "certutil.exe", "curl.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| summarize Executions = count(), Commands = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by bin(Timestamp, 15m), DeviceName, AccountName
| order by Timestamp asc, Executions desc

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where tolower(InitiatingProcessFileName) in (SCProcs)
| where AccountName in~ ("system", "nt authority\\system")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe", "regsvr32.exe", "msiexec.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")

kql.name: Microsoft Defender exclusion added (SCKit pre-staging)
kql.description: Untested. Installation scripts added Defender exclusions before deploying payloads. Any exclusion added by a remote-management parent is high-signal; exclusions are rare and deliberate in most estates.
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference", "Set-MpPreference", "ExclusionPath", "ExclusionProcess", "ExclusionExtension", "MpCmdRun.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Exclusion", "DisableRealtimeMonitoring", "DisableIOAVProtection")
| extend ViaRemoteTool = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwise"), "YES", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ViaRemoteTool, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName
| order by ViaRemoteTool desc, Timestamp desc

kql.name: Second / unauthorised ScreenConnect client installed
kql.description: Untested. The campaign installed a rogue ScreenConnect client alongside the legitimate one for redundant access. Replace the AuthorisedInstance string with your own instance identifier to make this precise.

let AuthorisedInstance = "REPLACE-WITH-YOUR-INSTANCE-ID";
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(21d)
| where FileName has_any ("ScreenConnect.Client", "ScreenConnect.WindowsClient", "ConnectWiseControl.Client", "ScreenConnect.ClientSetup")

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| extend Unexpected = iff(FolderPath has AuthorisedInstance, "expected", "REVIEW")

kql.name: Burst detection - same command across many endpoints in a short window
kql.description: Untested. All observed infections occurred inside 90 minutes. This surfaces the pattern itself: one command line executing across an unusual number of distinct devices in a short period, which is how mass push via a hijacked console looks in telemetry.
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwise")
| summarize DeviceCount = dcount(DeviceName), Devices = make_set(DeviceName, 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by ProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 90m)
| where DeviceCount >= 5
| extend SpreadMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| project Timestamp, DeviceCount, SpreadMinutes, FirstSeen, LastSeen, ProcessCommandLine, Devices
| order by DeviceCount desc

kql.name: ScreenConnect client beaconing to an unexpected relay
kql.description: Untested. A rogue client calls home to the attacker's relay, not yours. Add your legitimate relay FQDN(s) to the allowlist; everything else from a ScreenConnect process warrants investigation.
kql.query:

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(21d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwise")
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl) or isnotempty(RemoteIP)
| extend Host = tolower(coalesce(RemoteUrl, RemoteIP))
| where not (Host has_any (KnownRelays))
| summarize Connections = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by Host, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemotePort
| order by Connections desc

On 13 November 2026 the FBI issued FLASH-20261113-001 on ARTEX, an open-source large-language-model-driven agentic platform built for autonomous penetration testing and now, per the Bureau, weaponised by a range of malicious cyber actors since at least August 2026 to automate multiple phases of intrusion at machine speed. The sectors the FBI names are finance, government, technology, defence, energy and healthcare - the UK public-sector and CNI footprint almost exactly. Two figures in the advisory are the ones worth carrying into a UK board or SIRO conversation. The first is speed: some intrusions moved from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. The second is availability: the FBI found more than 1,600 exposed ARTEX operator consoles on the internet in early November, and although the original GitHub repository was removed by its developer in October, the Bureau says the framework continues to circulate through forks, localised variations, archived copies and a commercial edition marketed as ARTEX PRO. Removal of a repository is not containment of a capability. Why this ranks sixth in a UK feed on a quiet Saturday is a matter of timing. On 3 November 2026 the NCSC's State of the Cyber Nation assessment judged it highly likely that AI would be used in a ransomware attack on UK critical infrastructure within two years - a judgement reported widely as a 2028 horizon. Ten days later a US federal agency published an advisory stating that agentic AI tooling has been in criminal use against government and energy targets since August. Those two statements are not in conflict, because they measure different things: the NCSC was forecasting AI-enabled ransomware against CNI specifically, while the FLASH describes AI-accelerated intrusion tradecraft more broadly. But the practical reading for a UK defender is that the forecast window has already begun to close from the near end, and planning assumptions built around 'two years to prepare' need revisiting now. The defensive consequence is concrete and it is mostly about time, not tooling. If targeting-to-privilege is three hours, then every control that depends on a human reading an alert during office hours is out of position - and a Saturday like today is exactly when that gap is widest for UK local government, trusts and smaller departments relying on business-hours SOC cover. The three mitigations the FBI puts first are unglamorous and all pre-date AI: inventory peripheral internet-facing systems (the things an agent finds first because nobody owns them), restrict Kudu/SCM and cloud administration endpoints (the management planes an agent pivots through), and enforce least privilege on application consent grants (the identity path that does not look like an exploit). Note what is not claimed here: this is a force-multiplier story, not a new vulnerability class. ARTEX chains known weaknesses faster than a human operator would; nothing in the advisory requires a new patch. Caveats: all detail is from search-result summaries and secondary reporting of the FLASH, including a SafeBreach coverage note and an OODAloop analysis - the primary FBI document at ic3.gov was not retrieved from this environment. One outlet's claim that Chinese models, particularly DeepSeek Flash, predominate in attacker-controlled deployments could not be corroborated against the advisory and is carried as unverified. A reported campaign affecting approximately 67,000 individuals in South Korea is likewise relayed from secondary coverage, and no UK victim of ARTEX-assisted activity has been named.
recommended_actions: Inventory peripheral internet-facing systems this week and name an owner for each. The FBI's first mitigation is the oldest one in security because agentic tooling finds unowned edge hosts, test estates and forgotten subdomains faster than your asset register is updated.

Restrict cloud management and deployment endpoints to known networks - Azure App Service Kudu/SCM, equivalent AWS and GCP administration endpoints, and any CI/CD deployment surface reachable from the internet. These are named in the advisory as pivot points.

Audit application consent grants and OAuth service principals in Entra ID: remove unused grants, block user consent to unverified publishers, and review any application with mail, file or directory-wide permissions. This is an identity path that produces no exploit telemetry at all.

Re-test your detection and response assumptions against a three-hour clock, not a three-day one. Specifically ask: on a Saturday, how long until a privilege-escalation alert is seen by a human, and what is automated containment authorised to do without one? For most UK local authorities and trusts the honest answer today is longer than three hours.

Prioritise automated containment for the high-confidence cases - disable account, revoke sessions, isolate device - rather than buying new detection. Against machine-speed intrusion the constraint is response latency, not visibility.

Check whether anyone inside your own organisation has deployed ARTEX or a fork for legitimate red-team or assurance work, and whether its console is internet-reachable. The FBI found over 1,600 exposed consoles; an exposed offensive-automation console in your own estate is both a compromise route and a governance problem.

Brief your SIRO, audit committee or board that the NCSC's two-year AI forecast of 3 November and this 13 November FBI advisory are consistent but describe different ends of the same trend, and that resilience investment timelines predicated on 2028 should be re-examined. Say plainly that no UK victim has been named.

Fold this into Cyber Security and Resilience Bill readiness rather than treating it as separate: a 24-hour significant-incident notification duty is materially harder to meet when intrusions complete in hours, which makes detection-to-decision time a compliance variable and not only a security one.

vulnerabilities.title: Cursor Marketplace Compromise Delivered a Trojanised Claude Code Extension (2.1.312 / 2.1.313) That Installed an SSH Backdoor on Load - Root Cause Was a Vendor-Exposed Fireworks AI Key and Unredacted Credentials in Shared Trace Data; Up to 5,000 Developers Could Have Received It and Uninstalling Is Not Remediation
vulnerabilities.vendor: Cursor (Anysphere) - marketplace cache compromise; Fireworks AI - exposed access key (root cause)
affected_products: Cursor IDE extension marketplace cache - served modified copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension on 29 October 2026 for approximately 11 hours
Trojanised extension versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 (malicious builds served from the Cursor marketplace cache only)
Developer workstations and build agents that requested those cached versions on 29 October 2026 - at most 5,000 users per Cursor
Cursor-issued access key held by Fireworks AI, and a read-only storage bucket shared with that vendor (initial access)
Select SaaS tools used by Cursor, reached using unredacted credentials found inside copied trace data (lateral movement)
NOT affected per Cursor: Anthropic's genuine Claude Code extension, the Open VSX registry, Cursor production systems and Cursor's official app signing keys
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government digital teams and UK corporate engineering estates, through the developer toolchain. Cursor published an incident update on 13 November 2026, picked up in mainstream security reporting on 14 November inside this window, confirming a chain that ends with a backdoored AI coding extension served from its own marketplace. The chain is worth following precisely because every link is a supply-chain pattern that UK organisations currently under-govern. Link one: an access key that Cursor had issued to its inference vendor Fireworks AI was exposed by Fireworks, and an attacker used it to copy data out of a read-only storage bucket Cursor shared with that vendor. Link two: some of the copied trace data contained unredacted credentials, and the attacker used those as a starting point to reach a number of SaaS tools Cursor itself uses. Link three: on 29 October the attacker used one of those stolen credentials to place modified copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension into the cache serving the Cursor extension marketplace. Versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 were live for roughly eleven hours, and Cursor states that at most 5,000 users who requested those specific cached versions that day could have received the malicious build - a ceiling on possible exposure, not a count of infections, and several outlets have reported it as though it were the latter. The payload is the part that determines today's work. It executed the moment the extension loaded, with no user interaction, and attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable the SSH service and open a reverse tunnel. Cursor says the tunnel step would normally fail without administrator rights, which limits severity on well-configured corporate builds but not on developer machines where local administrator is routine, and not on build agents and containers running as root. The planted key is identifiable: Cursor's notice names the key comment 'svc-telemetry', which is what to grep for in authorized_keys. The single most important operational point is that uninstalling the extension does not remediate the host, because the SSH key and startup entries persist independently of the extension - and that is exactly the step an organisation will skip if it reads only the headline. Cursor's own remediation has been substantial: inference traffic moved away from Fireworks, vendor access revoked, internal credentials rotated, the extension marketplace rebuilt, and secret scanning and network restrictions expanded. Cursor also reports that fewer than 0.01% of customers had exposed API credentials and that production systems and official signing keys were untouched, and that Anthropic's genuine extension and the Open VSX registry were not compromised - a distinction that matters for anyone checking whether their AI coding tooling is in scope. UK relevance is direct and growing. Cursor and Claude Code are in active use across UK government digital teams, GDS-adjacent delivery units and the technology sector, and a developer workstation is a high-value target: it holds cloud credentials, repository access, signing material and production access in a way a general office endpoint does not. Read this entry against the GitHub Actions credential-theft campaign this feed carried on 13 November and the ControlPlane finding that UK public-sector repositories contained live credentials: the common factor is not AI, it is that secrets keep arriving in telemetry, traces and repositories where nobody expects to find them, and that trace data shared with a vendor is production credential material. The exposure window has closed, so the residual risk is persistence on hosts that pulled the build on 29 October. Detail is from search-result summaries and secondary reporting of Cursor's own incident update; the Cursor notice was not retrieved directly from this environment, and no attacker attribution has been reported.
recommended_actions: Identify every host that ran Cursor on or after 29 October 2026 - developer workstations, build agents, containers and cloud dev environments - and check the Claude Code extension version history for 2.1.312 or 2.1.313.

On any host that may have loaded those versions, inspect ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (and root's) for an entry commented 'svc-telemetry' and for any key you cannot attribute to a named person; remove it and record the finding.

Do not treat uninstalling the extension as remediation - Cursor explicitly warns it is insufficient. Check whether the SSH service was enabled, whether any startup or login items were added, and whether a reverse tunnel process or listening service persists.

Rotate credentials present on affected developer hosts on the assumption of exposure: cloud access keys, personal access tokens, npm and package-registry tokens, SSH keys, kubeconfigs, and any .env or credential files in local project directories. A developer workstation compromise is a credential incident first.

Review the SSH configuration you deploy to engineering endpoints: on corporate builds, SSH server should not be enabled by default and inbound SSH should not be reachable; a reverse tunnel needs outbound egress, so check egress policy on developer VLANs too.

Constrain which extensions and marketplaces are permitted in IDEs across the organisation, pin extension versions where the tooling allows it, and treat the IDE extension marketplace as a software supply chain requiring the same governance as package registries.

Audit what your own vendors can read: the root cause was an access key you would have classified as low risk, held by an inference provider, giving read access to a bucket of trace data that contained unredacted credentials. Inventory which third parties hold keys to your telemetry and whether that telemetry is scrubbed of secrets before it leaves.

Add trace, log and telemetry stores to the scope of secret scanning, not just source repositories. This incident is a direct demonstration that credentials in observability data are production credentials.

State the exposure figure accurately in internal reporting: Cursor's 5,000 is a maximum number of users who could have received the build, and reporting it as a confirmed infection count will distort your own risk assessment.
